metadata.title: The impact of financial education in schools on the financial literacy of Brazilian students

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 public-use microdata for Brazil and constructs the financial literacy outcome as a weighted average of the ten plausible values using the Stata repest command. The authors state that final student sampling weights from PISA 2022 were applied to ensure nationally representative estimates. For quantile regression, they incorporate probability weights (using the same final student weights) and use standard analytical errors, explicitly noting that no bootstrap or replicate-weight procedures were used. The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete information in the outcome (PVFL) and key covariates required for propensity score matching and quantile regression; missingness is handled via exclusion rather than imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Starting from the initial PISA 2022 sample of 5491 students, the authors recoded OECD non-responses/invalid codes as missing, then excluded observations with missing values in the outcome (Plausible Values of Financial Literacy) and in key covariates used for propensity score matching and quantile regression. This complete-case restriction removed 2033 students (37.02%), yielding a final analytic sample of 3458 students. No additional trimming or winsorization was applied because PISA financial literacy scores are standardized and scaled by the OECD.

main_findings.target_variable: Financial literacy (PVFL; plausible value of financial literacy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: PSM (nearest neighbor n=5) ATT: +45.57 PVFL points (SE=3.85, t=11.82, 95% CI [38.02; 53.14]); Unmatched difference: +53.02 (SE=3.90, t=15.18, 95% CI [46.18; 59.86]). Matching quality: Pseudo-R2=0.000; LR χ2=6.65 (p=0.919). Rosenbaum sensitivity: robust up to γ=2.0 (p-crítico table).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy data for Brazilian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged financial education exposure at school (treated vs control) alongside observable characteristics such as financial education course outside school, gender, ESCS, grade repetition, and school quality to estimate the effect on PVFL, finding that school-based financial education is associated with an average increase of 45.57 PVFL points after matching. This indicates that consolidating financial education within the Brazilian school curriculum may substantially improve students’ financial literacy, though the estimates rely on PSM/quantile assumptions and cross-sectional self-reported exposure rather than randomized exposure.

main_findings.target_variable: Financial literacy by topic: Credit and indebtedness (PVFL)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy data for Brazilian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged observable characteristics (financial education course outside school, gender, ESCS, grade repetition, and school quality) to estimate the association between school exposure to the credit-and-indebtedness topic and PVFL, finding a positive and statistically significant ATT of +42.88 points after matching. This indicates that curriculum content focused on credit/debt and related everyday financial decisions may be a high-impact component for improving financial literacy, though causal interpretation remains conditional on PSM and cross-sectional measurement.

Using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy data for Brazilian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged observable characteristics (financial education course outside school, gender, ESCS, grade repetition, and school quality) to estimate the association between school exposure to investments content and PVFL, finding a positive and statistically significant ATT of +35.40 points after matching. This indicates that including investments-related concepts can improve financial literacy, with stronger gains for some parts of the proficiency distribution, suggesting that differentiated instructional support may be needed for students with lower prior knowledge.

main_findings.target_variable: Financial literacy by topic: Financial planning (PVFL)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy data for Brazilian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged observable characteristics (financial education course outside school, gender, ESCS, grade repetition, and school quality) to estimate the association between school exposure to financial planning content and PVFL, finding the largest positive and statistically significant ATT of +49.99 points after matching. This indicates that budgeting, wages, and retirement/pension planning topics are likely the most effective curriculum components for improving financial literacy across proficiency levels, informing BNCC-aligned material and teacher-training priorities.

main_findings.target_variable: Financial literacy by topic: General economic concepts (PVFL)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy data for Brazilian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged observable characteristics (financial education course outside school, gender, ESCS, grade repetition, and school quality) to estimate the association between school exposure to general economic concepts and PVFL, finding a positive and statistically significant ATT of +37.44 points after matching. This indicates that broader economic concepts can support financial literacy gains, but the non-linear quantile pattern suggests that instructional design may need to account for student proficiency to maximize benefits.

data.outcome_summary: This study estimates the impact of school-based financial education on financial literacy using PISA 2022 Financial Literacy microdata for Brazil (final analytic sample N=3458). The dependent variable is PVFL, constructed as a weighted average of the ten plausible values, and the main identification strategy is Propensity Score Matching (nearest neighbor with five neighbors) combined with quantile regression (UQTE). After matching, exposure to financial education topics at school is associated with an average increase of +45.57 PVFL points (SE=3.85; 95% CI [38.02; 53.14]), and the effect is robust to Rosenbaum sensitivity up to γ=2.0. Topic-specific results show the largest gains for Financial Planning (+49.99) and Credit & Debt (+42.88), with heterogeneous effects across the PVFL distribution. Limitations include cross-sectional measurement of exposure via student self-reports and reliance on PSM/ignorability assumptions rather than randomized treatment; the paper also does not use ML algorithms, so “ML” performance metrics are not applicable.
